questions.q: What happens when a team routes every alert through one queue at Sev1 urgency, regardless of real severity?
options: A flood of low-severity noise at high urgency teaches the on-call engineer to ignore pages, the opposite of what alerting should do
Alertmanager automatically converts it into three separate severity tiers
Nothing changes — severity tiers only affect which dashboard a panel appears on
It permanently disables paging for that service
questions.explain: Treating every alert as equally urgent trains responders to tune pages out, which is exactly the alert-fatigue problem this lesson is about avoiding.

questions.q: What is label-based routing, and what problem does it solve?
options: It encrypts alert payloads so only authorized teams can read them
It automatically rewrites an alert's severity based on time of day
It matches an alert's labels (service, team, severity) against routing rules so the team that owns the failing component is paged, not a generic on-call rotation
It replaces the need for a severity tier entirely
questions.explain: Routing on labels like team and service sends an alert to whoever actually owns the failing piece, instead of wasting time paging a team that can't act on it.

questions.q: In the Alertmanager config shown, what does `group_by: ["alertname", "service"]` achieve?
options: It deletes alerts for that service after one hour
It collapses many individual firing alerts for the same root cause into one notification instead of paging once per affected instance
It forces every alert for that service to Sev1 severity
It disables routing for any alert missing a service label
questions.explain: Grouping by alertname and service is the deduplication mechanism — many alerts from the same underlying problem become one notification.

questions.q: How does a silence differ from an inhibit rule?
options: A silence only works for Sev1 alerts; inhibit rules only work for Sev3 alerts
They are two names for the exact same mechanism in Alertmanager
An inhibit rule requires manual approval from the on-call engineer every time it fires
A silence is a human-declared, time-bounded rule for planned maintenance; an inhibit rule automatically suppresses one alert because a related alert is already firing
questions.explain: A silence is created ahead of known work (a deploy, a maintenance window); inhibition is automatic, suppressing a dependent alert (like HighLatency) when a related one (like ServiceDown) is already active.

questions.q: In the sample routing tree, why does a critical alert labeled team="payments" reach the payments on-call pager rather than the checkout team?
options: Prometheus assigns alerts to teams randomly to balance on-call load
Because the routing rule matches on the alert's severity and team labels, and only the matching nested route's receiver gets notified
Because payments alerts are always treated as higher severity than checkout alerts
Because the default-slack receiver only accepts payments alerts
questions.explain: The nested route with matchers for severity="critical" and team="payments" is what directs that specific alert to payments-oncall-page.
